key_risks.description: Q2 2026 operating profit includes $392 million of expected IEEPA tariff recoveries booked in cost of goods sold. These sit in receivables, not collected cash. Further recoveries were not deemed probable at June 30, 2026, CBP timing is uncertain, and the outlook excludes additional recoveries. Underlying operating margin is therefore about 19.0% rather than the reported 20.9%, and the recovery will not repeat in the second half.

Tariff costs remain heavy. Management expects about $2.2 billion for 2026 excluding IEEPA recoveries (roughly double the 2025 level) and about $600 million in Q3 2026. Unless pricing and volume offset them, these costs pressure margins in the second half.

Dealer inventory rose $2.6 billion in the first half of 2026 vs $0.2 billion a year earlier. Management expects a Construction Industries dealer inventory build of over $1.0 billion in Q4 2026 and an unfavorable dealer-inventory effect on Construction Industries volume in the second half vs 2025. Reported growth may overstate end-user demand and decelerate.

Shareholder returns exceeded cash generation. Dividends paid of $1,399 million and share repurchases of $6,522 million in the first half compare with consolidated operating cash flow of $6,241 million. Cash and cash equivalents fell to $6,713 million from $9,980 million, and Financial Products debt issuance of $7,363 million exceeded repayments of $4,744 million. Sustaining this pace relies on drawing down cash and on finance-arm leverage.

bull_case: Power & Energy is becoming a structural growth platform. First-half 2026 Power Generation sales rose 34%, driven by data-center applications across large reciprocating engines and turbines. Q2 Power & Energy sales rose 17% to $8,238 million and segment profit rose about 30% to $2,027 million.

Backlog provides revenue visibility. Firm backlog was about $72.1 billion at June 30, 2026, up about $9.4 billion in one quarter, led by Power & Energy. Management says capacity expansion is progressing and expects higher throughput in the second half of 2026. Large orders such as the 2 GW AIP order and turbine orders extending toward 2030 point to multi-year demand.

Underlying margins expanded even after stripping out one-time items. Q2 operating margin was 20.9%; excluding the $392 million IEEPA recoveries it is about 19.0%, still roughly 170 bp above the 17.3% of Q2 2025. First-half operating profit rose 36% on sales growth of 23%.

Earnings power is scaling quickly. First-half profit of consolidated and affiliated companies rose 47% to $6,141 million and Q2 diluted EPS rose 68% to $7.77 (adjusted $8.17). A shrinking diluted share count (462.5 million vs 471.5 million) adds a further tailwind.

Management raised the sales outlook to growth in the mid-to-high teens for 2026, expects strong growth across all primary segments from volume and favorable price realization, and expects services revenue to grow.

Further upside is possible but unmodeled. The outlook excludes any additional IEEPA recoveries (a $1.2 billion long-term receivable for overpayments is carried), and partnerships such as Hunt Energy and AIP suggest optionality toward recurring, higher-margin power-solutions revenue.
Shareholder returns are strong: $6,522 million of buybacks and $1,399 million of dividends in the first half, with the stated goal of returning substantially all MP&E free cash flow.
bear_case: Q2 quality of earnings is flattered. $392 million of expected IEEPA tariff recoveries (a receivable, not cash) lifted Q2 operating profit. Incremental margin falls from about 36% to about 26% without it, and the outlook assumes no repeat in the second half.

Tariff costs are a growing offset. Management expects about $2.2 billion in 2026 excluding recoveries (roughly double 2025) and about $600 million in Q3, and Q3 guidance flags unfavorable manufacturing costs and higher SG&A/R&D in Power & Energy.

Dealer-inventory timing may inflate reported growth. Dealer inventory rose $2.6 billion in the first half vs $0.2 billion a year earlier, Construction Industries sales rose 35% in Q2, and management expects an unfavorable second-half Construction Industries volume effect and a Q4 build of over $1.0 billion. Reported growth rates are likely to decelerate.

Capital returns outrun cash generation. First-half dividends plus buybacks of about $7.9 billion exceeded consolidated operating cash flow of $6.2 billion. Cash fell by $3.3 billion to $6,713 million and Financial Products debt rose, so continued returns rely on cash drawdown and leverage.

Cash conversion is timing-assisted. Customer advances of +$2,576 million flattered operating cash flow while receivables (-$3,182 million) and inventories (-$2,553 million) absorbed cash. An unwind of advances would hurt reported free cash flow.

Valuation leaves little room. Consensus FY2026 EPS of roughly $27 and FY2027 of roughly $33 embeds a sustained step-up in earnings, with the stock near 25x forward earnings per recent coverage, and the Q2 beat included non-repeatable benefits.

Off-balance-sheet exposure is growing: guarantees rose to $669 million from $458 million in six months, with some unlimited guarantees that cannot be quantified. Rising restructuring costs ($300–350 million expected in 2026) add further drag.

what_to_watch.text:
**IEEPA Tariff Recovery and Underlying Margin:** Q2 operating profit included $392 million of expected IEEPA tariff recoveries booked in cost of goods sold. Excluding it, operating margin is about 19.0% vs the 20.9% reported, and incremental margin falls from about 36% to about 26%. That said, even the ex-recovery margin is roughly 170 bp above the 17.3% of Q2 2025, so underlying expansion is real, and a $1.2 billion long-term overpayment receivable is carried that guidance excludes.

-> Monitor adjusted operating margin ex-recoveries, the conversion of the recovery receivable into cash, and any change in management's stance on additional IEEPA claims.

**Dealer Inventory and Second-Half Volume:** Dealer inventory rose $2.6 billion in the first half vs $0.2 billion a year earlier, and management expects a Construction Industries build of over $1.0 billion in Q4 plus an unfavorable second-half volume effect vs 2025. This raises the risk that first-half sales growth of 23% (volume +$5.4 billion, price +$1.0 billion) overstates end-user demand. However, the $2.4 billion year-over-year swing is only about a third of the $7.1 billion sales increase, a $72.1 billion firm backlog (up $9.4 billion in the quarter, led by Power & Energy) is not explained by restocking, and the air-pocket risk is concentrated in Construction Industries rather than across the whole growth rate.

-> Monitor Construction Industries dealer-inventory change, dealer months-of-supply commentary, and how management sizes the second-half volume headwind.

**Capital Return Versus Cash Generation:** First-half buybacks of $6,522 million and dividends of $1,399 million (about $7.9 billion) exceeded MP&E free cash flow of roughly $5.7 billion and consolidated operating cash flow of $6,241 million. Cash fell from $9,980 million to $6,713 million, and Financial Products issued $7,363 million of debt against $4,744 million of repayments. On the other hand, much of the Financial Products borrowing funds finance receivables rather than shareholder returns, and management's goal of returning substantially all MP&E free cash flow over time while holding a mid-A rating could be read as confidence in the earnings trajectory.

-> Monitor the pace of repurchases, MP&E net debt and cash balance, and management commentary on capital return priorities versus capacity capex.

**Power & Energy Growth and Backlog Conversion:** Power Generation sales rose 34% in the first half on data-center demand, Q2 Power & Energy segment profit rose to $2,027 million from $1,554 million, and firm backlog reached about $72.1 billion, up about $9.4 billion in the quarter. Management expects higher throughput in the second half as capacity expansion progresses, and large orders (such as 2 GW for a hyperscale AI campus) extend visibility into 2027 and beyond. That said, the firm backlog is only the portion believed to be firm and growth is capacity-constrained, so conversion to revenue and the timing of additions matter as much as order intake.

-> Monitor Power & Energy backlog composition, throughput and capacity-expansion milestones, and Power Generation sales growth against the 34% first-half pace.

**Tariff Costs, Pricing and Third-Quarter Margins:** Management expects about $2.2 billion of 2026 tariff costs excluding IEEPA recoveries (roughly double the 2025 level) and about $600 million in Q3. It guides to Q3 Power & Energy profit benefiting from higher volume and favorable price realization, but partly offset by unfavorable manufacturing costs and higher SG&A/R&D. The first-half operating margin of 19.4% vs 17.6% supports expansion, but it includes the one-time recovery, so durability still has to be shown on an ex-recovery basis.

-> Monitor the realized price-versus-cost spread, Q3 tariff cost vs the $600 million estimate, and segment margins excluding recoveries.

**Quality of Operating Cash Flow:** Consolidated operating cash flow of $6,241 million roughly matches profit of $6,141 million, but it includes $2,576 million of customer advances while receivables absorbed $3,182 million and inventories $2,553 million. Customer advances can reverse, so the jump in MP&E free cash flow from about $2.6 billion to $5.7 billion is partly timing. On the other hand, the advances reflect strong order intake and backlog growth, which is consistent with healthy demand rather than stress.

-> Monitor customer advances, receivables and inventory build, and whether operating cash flow tracks profit once the tariff-recovery receivable is collected.

**Guarantee Exposure and Financial Products:** Maximum potential future payments under guarantees rose to $669 million from $458 million in six months, and certain unlimited guarantees cannot be quantified. Financial Products long-term debt due after one year rose to $21,384 million from $20,018 million, while segment profit improved to $328 million from $248 million in Q2. Credit performance is supportive today, but growing off-balance-sheet exposure alongside a dealer channel build deserves scrutiny.

-> Monitor the guarantee disclosure, Financial Products past-dues and write-offs, and finance-arm leverage trends.

**Consensus Expectations and Valuation:** Street estimates call for FY2026 EPS of roughly $27 and FY2027 of roughly $33, with Q3 2026 near $7.03, after a Q2 adjusted EPS of $8.17 that included the tariff recovery. Management's raised sales outlook (mid-to-high teens growth) and rising backlog support those numbers. However, estimates may be extrapolating a Q2 margin that benefited from a non-recurring item, and the stock trades at a demanding forward multiple.

-> Monitor guidance language on the full-year margin outlook and how analysts treat the $392 million recovery in their estimates.

hypotheses_explored.summary: It does not cover them. H1 2026 MP&E free cash flow was $5.698B, while dividends ($1.399B) plus buybacks ($6.522B) totaled about $7.92B, a shortfall of roughly $2.2B. Management says its goal is to return substantially all MP&E free cash flow, but in H1 it returned well over 100% of that figure. The return program is being financed by cash drawdown and FP leverage, not by free cash flow. Confidence is high because all the figures come directly from the filing's cash flow tables and MD&A.

hypotheses_explored.question: How much of the H1 2026 MP&E operating cash flow reflects durable earnings versus timing items such as customer advances and working capital swings, and would that flatter the cash conversion story?
hypotheses_explored.summary: Probably yes, in part. Consolidated operating cash flow of $6.241B is roughly equal to profit of $6.141B, so consolidated conversion looks adequate. But MP&E operating cash flow of $7.011B includes a $2.576B customer advances line, and working capital was a large drag: inventories absorbed $2.553B and trade receivables absorbed $3.182B. Those advances can reverse, so this half's MP&E cash flow is not a clean run-rate. The MP&E free cash flow jump from $2.575B to $5.698B therefore needs to be treated as partly timing. This is a quality-of-earnings concern to raise on the call, though the filing does not quantify how much of the advance is expected to unwind. Confidence is moderate because the advance line is read from the consolidating table column and the filing does not state the reversal profile.

hypotheses_explored.question: Is the Q2 2026 earnings beat a durable step-up in earnings power, or is it flattered by a one-time $392M IEEPA tariff recovery and a $2.6B dealer inventory build that the Street is treating as run-rate?
hypotheses_explored.summary: Consensus is extrapolating Q2 2026 adjusted EPS of $8.17 and a 21.9% adjusted operating margin as the new base. My contrarian read is that the quality of that beat is weaker than it looks. The $392M IEEPA recovery is a non-recurring item booked in cost of goods sold, and the filing says further refunds are not yet probable, so the upside is not in the base case. Separately, dealer inventory rose $2.6B in the first half of 2026 versus $200M a year earlier, so part of the volume growth reflects channel loading rather than end-user demand. If I strip out the recovery, the margin gain is much smaller, and the Street's FY2026 and FY2027 estimates (roughly $27 and $33 EPS) look aggressive.

hypotheses_explored.question: Is the data-center power generation story already priced in, or is there an under-discussed cost drag from tariffs that the bull case assumes away?
hypotheses_explored.summary: The bull narrative is that data-center gensets and turbines drive a multi-year growth and margin expansion cycle. Power Generation sales grew 34% in the first half, and firm backlog reached $72.1B, up $9.4B in one quarter. The hidden assumption is that pricing and margins hold while tariff costs stay elevated. Management is guiding to about $2.2B of 2026 tariff cost excluding any IEEPA refunds, which is roughly double the 2025 level of about $1.0B. Capacity is also being added quickly, and the backlog includes a large non-firm component. The risk is that the consensus is paying for peak-cycle power margins while assuming tariff costs fall away. The strongest contrarian signal is the gap between the segment's volume growth and what the cost base will absorb.
